characters: Kojo: a nine-year-old Ghanaian boy with short curly hair, bright observant eyes, wearing a yellow t-shirt, khaki shorts, sturdy walking shoes, and a small green field notebook.
Ranger Akosua: Kojo’s aunt, a wildlife ranger in her thirties wearing a neat olive-green ranger shirt, bush hat, and binoculars around her neck.
Papa Kwesi: a friendly neighbouring cocoa farmer in a checked work shirt who greets them at the forest edge.

narrationPlan.pace: Medium-slow (about 115 words per minute) for Primary 3–4 learners.
notes: Bring gentle wonder to the canopy and forest-floor discoveries.
Pronounce Kojo, Akosua, Kwesi, Kakum, odum and wawa clearly.

music: Optional low-key soft piano ambience (user-togglable in reader header; off by default).
culturalNotes: Highlights Kakum National Park and Ghana’s cocoa agro-ecology accurately.
reviewQuestions: Confirm species names and reading level for Primary 3–4 with a Ghanaian science educator.

pages.brief: Morning mist in Kakum rainforest. Kojo (9, yellow t-shirt, khaki shorts, green notebook) walking on a forest path beside Ranger Akosua (olive-green ranger uniform, bush hat, binoculars).
pages.narration: Fresh morning energy. Curious tone for Kojo’s question.

pages.brief: Ranger Akosua touching the massive buttress roots of a tall odum rainforest tree while Kojo gazes up into the sunlit green canopy.
Close view of a cocoa tree trunk with small pale flowers and golden cocoa pods; Ranger Akosua and Kojo peering closely while Papa Kwesi smiles nearby.
pages.narration: Quiet amazement. Slow and clear on "pollination".

pages.brief: On the Kakum canopy walkway high in the sunlit treetops, Ranger Akosua points to glowing green leaves while Kojo holds the safety rail and smiles.
pages.narration: Bright and uplifting. Clear emphasis on "producers".

pages.brief: In the lush rainforest canopy, two Diana monkeys with distinctive white chest/beard fur eat wild figs on a branch while a large hornbill bird glides across the background.
pages.narration: Lively and vivid. Pause briefly after "Suddenly, the branches rustled!"

pages.brief: Split-focus rainforest scene: a bright green tree frog on a glossy leaf in the foreground, with Kojo and Ranger Akosua looking up toward a crowned eagle soaring above the treetops.
pages.narration: Clear explanation, showing how each creature connects in the food web.

pages.brief: On the damp shaded forest floor, Kojo kneels with his notebook beside a fallen log covered in cream-and-orange bracket fungi, moss, and a brown millipede.
Close view of Ranger Akosua and Kojo pointing at tiny green tree seedlings sprouting from dark rich humus soil right beside the mushroom-covered log.
pages.narration: Warm and appreciative of the tiny recyclers. Clear on "decomposers" and "decomposition".

pages.brief: Beside a clear sunlit rainforest stream, Ranger Akosua and Kojo crouch to look at large round forest elephant footprints in the damp bank.
At the sunlit forest edge, Kojo proudly holds up his open green notebook showing a simple circle of nature drawings (sun, leaf, flower, mushroom, no text) to a beaming Ranger Akosua.
pages.narration: Proud, warm, and satisfying conclusion. Pause before "The end".

teacherGuide.overview: Set in and around Kakum National Park in Ghana’s Central Region, this story introduces Primary 3–4 learners to habitats, producers, pollination (cocoa midges), seed dispersal (straw-coloured fruit bats and Diana monkeys), food webs, decomposition, and forest conservation.
learningGoals: Identify different forest habitats (canopy, forest floor, stream) and the Ghanaian organisms that live in them.
Explain how producers, pollinators, seed dispersers, predators and decomposers depend on one another in a food web.
Describe how protecting forests supports nearby farms, clean streams and soil health.

beforeReading: Ask: "Have you ever seen a mushroom growing on an old log or insects visiting flowers? What were they doing?"
Show where Kakum National Park is in Ghana’s Central Region.
whileReading: After page 3, ask learners why cocoa farmers need tiny insects in the leaf litter near their trees.
After page 8, ask how fungi and termites act as the forest’s cleaning and recycling team.
afterReading: Take a 10-minute walk around the school compound to spot one producer (plant), one pollinator (insect/bird), and one decomposer (ant/millipede/fungus, look, do not touch).
discussion: Why did Kojo at first think only the big trees mattered?
What would happen to young tree saplings if there were no fungi, termites or bacteria on the forest floor?
How does a healthy forest help farmers like Papa Kwesi who live near the park?
reflection: Why do even the smallest creatures in a community deserve care and respect?
What can our class do to keep trees and soil healthy around our school?

mathsExtension.task: Kojo counted 8 Diana monkeys in one odum tree and 6 in a wawa tree. How many monkeys did he see in all?
A cocoa tree had 24 pods. Papa Kwesi harvested 15 ripe pods. How many pods were left on the tree?

support: Draw a simple 3-step chain (Sunlight → Fig Tree → Diana Monkey) before adding decomposers.
stretch: Draw a 6-organism Kakum food web with arrows showing how energy and nutrients move.

culturalNotes: Kojo (boy born on Monday) and Akosua (girl born on Sunday) are Akan day names; Kwesi is a boy born on Sunday.
Kakum National Park in the Central Region is famous for its moist evergreen rainforest and canopy walkway.
localiseThis: Supplement Kakum rainforest examples with local savannah, coastal wetland or farm species from your school’s district.

factCheck.claim: Cocoa flowers (Theobroma cacao) are primarily pollinated by tiny biting midges (family Ceratopogonidae, especially Forcipomyia species) that breed in moist leaf litter.
factCheck.explanation: Unlike large bees, tiny Ceratopogonid midges are small enough to enter the intricate hood of cocoa flowers and transfer pollen.
factCheck.reference: Cocoa Research Institute of Ghana (CRIG) & FAO Pollination Services for Sustainable Agriculture.

factCheck.claim: Kakum National Park provides habitat for African forest elephants (Loxodonta cyclotis), Diana monkeys (Cercopithecus diana), yellow-casqued hornbills (Ceratogymna elata), and trees such as odum (Milicia excelsa) and wawa (Triplochiton scleroxylon).
factCheck.explanation: All named species are documented native inhabitants of Ghana’s Upper Guinean moist evergreen forest zone at Kakum.
factCheck.reference: Forestry Commission of Ghana (Wildlife Division) Kakum National Park Biodiversity Records; IUCN Red List.

factCheck.claim: Straw-coloured fruit bats (Eidolon helvum) disperse seeds across West African forests and savannahs, and fungi, termites, millipedes and bacteria decompose dead wood into soil nutrients.
factCheck.explanation: Eidolon helvum is a keystone seed disperser for reforestation in Ghana; saprotrophic fungi and detritivores mineralise organic matter.
factCheck.reference: University of Ghana Department of Animal Biology and Conservation Science; UNESCO MAB Biosphere Reserve Studies.

pronunciation.guidance: "ah-KOH-swah"; a three-syllable "ah-KOH-soo-ah" may be more accurate.
reviewerNotes: Two or three syllables at the end? Please decide.
